$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 3 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot (-2)-1\cdot 3}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -3 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -3 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

![](images/1b/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{array}\right].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1 & -3 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 & -1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1 & -3 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 6 & -2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1 & -3 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1 & 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -1\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={\begin{bmatrix}5 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot (-1)-3\cdot (-2)}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -3 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -3 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -3 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & -9 \\ 10 & -5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -3 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & -11 \\ 5 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

To determine the amount of powder that must be dissolved in $8.6$ liters of water, we have to multiply $8.6$ by $5.5.$

We proceed by multiplying the two numbers just as we would with whole numbers.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  &  &  & \,\,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{3} \\ \boxed{3}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{} \\ \boxed{0}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  &  &  & \,\,\,\,8\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,.6\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,.5\,\,\,\, \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,7\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We now count the total number of decimal places in the two factors.

There is $1$ decimal place in $8.6$ and there is $1$ decimal place in $5.5.$
Therefore, their product will have $1+1=2$ decimal places.

So, we take our value of $4730$ and add a decimal point to make a number with $2$ decimal places.

$$
47\,\overset{↓}{.}\,\,\,\underbrace{30}_{2\text{ digits}}
$$

Hence, $8.6\times 5.5=47.30=47.3.$

We conclude that $47.3$ grams of powder must be dissolved in $8.6$ liters of water.

Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-6.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-6.$ Computing $A-(-6)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+6I & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}+6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ \frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\end{bmatrix}
$$
